claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is in an engineered hierarchical-heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The alloy contains spatial grain-orientation variations.
High-throughput in situ nanoindentation mapping can obtain local load-displacement responses across the alloy's heterogeneous regions.
Sub-micron EBSD can provide local crystallographic descriptors, including grain orientations, for the heterogeneous alloy.
EBSD measurements can capture the alloy's local chemical fluctuations.
Nanoindentation load-displacement responses capture spatial variations in local stiffness and yielding behavior.
Local mechanical responses directly reflect the underlying hierarchical chemical heterogeneities.
A physics-informed machine-learning model calibrated using bulk tensile and fracture tests can learn correlations between local descriptors and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Using experimentally measured local descriptors will reduce the need for extensive first-principles and CALPHAD calculations.
The proposed model will predict bulk Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Prediction errors will be approximately 20–25% lower than those of approaches relying solely on thermophysical parameters.
The proposed method will decrease overall computational effort by approximately 70–80%.
The predictions will remain reliable when nanoindentation and EBSD spatial resolution is sufficient to resolve the hierarchical fluctuations.
Current thermophysical-parameter, CALPHAD, and first-principles methods have high computational demands.
Current methods have limited accuracy for predicting fracture toughness.
The methodology will lose reliability when the microstructural heterogeneity scale is below the effective spatial resolution of nanoindentation or EBSD.
The methodology will lose reliability if deformation mechanisms absent from the local descriptors dominate the bulk response.
A blinded prospective benchmark will use 50 independently prepared HfNbTiVAl10 samples and compare model predictions with standardized room-temperature tensile and fracture measurements.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if predictions for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness consistently deviate by more than ±10% from measured values across the blinded set.
